# Encryption and Globalization 15 Years Later: End-to-End Encryption and the Third Round of the "Going Dark" Debate

## Abstract

This Article updates and expands on 2012 research on encryption and globalization, analyzing what the authors call "Round 3" of the Going Dark Debate: the current controversies over end-to-end encryption (E2EE). Governments around the world have proposed, and in some cases enacted, laws limiting E2EE for law enforcement and national security purposes. This Article explains the underlying technologies and market developments for a law and policy audience to assess those proposals critically. The Article proceeds in three parts tracking three rounds of the Going Dark Debate. Round 1 covers the Crypto Wars of the 1990s, when U.S. export controls on strong encryption ultimately fell in 1999. Round 2 covers the period roughly 2010 to 2015, when encryption-in-transit became widespread but lawful access remained available through cloud providers, giving rise to what the authors called a "golden age of surveillance" rather than a period of going dark. Round 3 addresses the current debate over E2EE, where no entity between sender and recipient can read the plaintext. The Article's first major contribution is identifying five technically distinct scenarios for how E2EE operates in practice, each with different implications for lawful access. These scenarios reveal a substantial gap between the assumption that E2EE categorically blocks lawful access 1 by co-authors Swire and Ahmad, and the companion 2012 article by Swire on “From Real-Time Intercepts to Stored Records: Why Encryption Drives the Government to Seek Access to the Cloud.”

## INTRODUCTION

The 2020's have seen a revival in the long-running debate about whether and how governments will impose limits on effective encryption. Governments around the globe seek to gain "lawful access" to information, notably to assist law enforcement and national security investigations. Depending on how the technology is deployed, encryption may block these sorts of investigations from gaining such access. In response, governments since the rise of the commercial Internet have proposed, and sometimes implemented, laws that restrict the use of encryption.

This Article updates and expands the 2012 article "Encryption and Globalization," 1 by co-authors Swire and Ahmad, and the companion 2012 article by Swire on "From Real-Time Intercepts to Stored Records: Why Encryption Drives the Government to Seek Access to the Cloud." 2 As with the two previous articles, this Article explains the underlying technologies and market developments for a law and policy audience. A clear understanding of these technological and market realities, in turn, equips law and policy readers to assess new proposals to limit and otherwise govern the use of strong encryption. Notably, this sort of understanding is vital for assessing government claims that encryption limits are needed to provide lawful access for law enforcement and national security investigations. 3 art II of the Article summarizes key lessons from the "Crypto Wars" of the 1990's, when law and policy leaders became more involved in cryptography debates, that until then were primarily held in the technical community. 4 As the commercial Internet began to develop in the 1990's, export of strong encryption from the United States was illegal, with the stated goal of maintaining lawful access for law enforcement and national security investigations. In this first round of encryption controversy that engaged many law and policy leaders, three related arguments supported the use of strong encryption: a privacy argument to maintain the confidentiality of communications; a cybersecurity argument stressing that effective encryption was necessary to protect important activity on the Internet; and a commercial argument that strong encryption was necessary for U.S.-based companies to sell encryption products and compete effectively online. This round of the argument, focused on U.S. policy, effectively ended in 1999 when the U.S. government shifted position and approved the global export of almost all encryption.

Part III of the Article explains the legal and policy debates that emerged as encryption became globally controversial by the time of the 2012 articles. By then, government agencies were facing newly prevalent use of encryption-in-transit for email, web, and many other communications. To describe the concern of government agencies, FBI lawyer Valerie Caproni introduced the term "going dark" in 2011 testimony, and the phrase became the defining image for law enforcement's belief it was losing visibility into encrypted content.

The 2012 articles examined how technical and market realities had changed. Lawful access continued to be possible from cloud providers. First, encryption policy should be developed with consideration of the "least trusted country;" that is, a proposed limit on encryption should be normatively evaluated on how one would like that power to exist in the country one trusts the least. This perspective was vital, because encryption broken for the benefit of one country would also be broken for the benefit of other countries, including those one trusts the least. Second, we argued that government agencies were not "going dark" when it came to their surveillance powers; instead, we had entered what we called a "golden age of surveillance." Law enforcement and other government agencies had unprecedented and sweeping capabilities to gather information about individuals. The normative claims by governments of the need to limit encryption were thus far weaker than often believed.

Part IV of this Article analyzes what we call "Round 3 of the Going Dark Debates." The most important technical and market change since 2012 comes from multiple uses for "end-to-end encryption" (E2EE). We define E2EE as having no one between the sender (Alice) and recipient (Bob) who can read the plaintext (the content of the communication). 6 nder the architecture prevalent in 2012, the cloud companies positioned between Alice and Bob had access to the plaintext, allowing governments to use lawful access to seek evidence held by those providers. By contrast, with E2EE, there is no entity between Alice and Bob who can read the content of the communications. Even the cloud companies only have access to encrypted communications, so lawful access would no longer work when sought from the cloud providers.

Plaintext is defined as "[u]nencrypted information that may be input to an encryption operation. 6 Part IV discusses five scenarios for E2EE, including the scenario we call "true" or "implicitly assumed" E2EE. In that scenario there is E2EE as defined in the text, with no one between Alice and Bob able to read the content. There is also no mechanism for anyone other than Bob to read the content once the content arrives to Bob. The other four scenarios all involve E2EE in the sense that no one between Alice and Bob can read the content, but there is some other way that lawful access may be possible because the content of the communication may become available to someone other than Bob.

Governments around the globe in recent years have proposed limits on E2EE. Supporters of these proposals highlight what they consider the unprecedented lack of lawful access to communications protected by E2EE. Our analysis offers reasons for great caution about claims to unprecedented and decisive loss of access for law enforcement and national security investigations. As one contribution of this Article, we explain at least five distinct scenarios that all constitute E2EE with very different legal and policy implications. We also emphasize a point we have not seen elsewhere, that E2EE is used for many of the most important and widespread protocols used on the modern Internet. Therefore, any law or policy proposal that limits E2EE risks pervasively undermining the cybersecurity of modern computing.

In the conclusion, in Part V, we underscore the continued importance of the two lessons from Round 2 of the Going Dark Debates -the risk posed by the least trusted country, and the continuing ways that we live in a Golden Age of Surveillance. Encryption is far more widely used than in 2012, for compelling reasons. Great skepticism should continue to apply to the claims of law enforcement and national security agencies that the law should restrict use of effective encryption.

Round 1: The Crypto Wars of the 1990s

Part II explains how the technical architecture of the early Internet was insecure, leading to strong arguments for users being able to encrypt their communications through the Internet. Although U.S. law enforcement and national security agencies argued vigorously for placing limits on use of strong encryption, the "Crypto Wars" of the 1990's ended with broad legal authorization for such encryption.
